etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English olde, ald, from Old English ald, eald (“old, aged, ancient, antique, primeval”), from Proto-West Germanic *ald, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz (“grown-up”), originally a participle form, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós (“grown, tall, big”). Cognate with Scots auld (“old”), North Frisian ool, ual, uul (“old”), Saterland Frisian oold (“old”), West Frisian âld (“old”), Dutch oud (“old”), Low German old (“old”), German alt (“old”), Swedish äldre (“older, elder”), Icelandic eldri (“older, elder”), Latin altus (“high, tall, grown big, lofty”). Related to eld.

definitions.definition: Of a living being, having lived for most of the expected years.
Of a perishable item, having existed for most of, or more than, its shelf life.
Of a species or language, belonging to a lineage that is distantly related others
Of an object, concept, relationship, etc., having existed for a relatively long period of time.

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], chapter 1, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: They burned the old gun that used to stand in the dark corner up in the garret, close to the stuffed fox that always grinned so fiercely. Perhaps the reason why he seemed in such a ghastly rage was that he did not come by his death fairly. Otherwise his pelt would not have been so perfect. And why else was he put away up there out of sight?—and so magnificent a brush as he had too.

definitions.definition: Having been used and thus no longer new or unused.
Having existed or lived for the specified time.
Former, previous.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self again; for, even after she had conquered her love for the Celebrity, the mortification of having been jilted by him remained.
But over my old life, a new life had formed.

definitions.definition: That is no longer in existence.
Obsolete; out-of-date.
Familiar.

quote.citation: 1991, Stephen Fry, chapter III, in The Liar, London: William Heinemann, →ISBN, page 26:
quote.text: Adrian thought it worth while to try out his new slang. ‘I say, you fellows, here's a rum go. Old Biffo was jolly odd this morning. He gave me a lot of pi-jaw about slacking and then invited me to tea. No rotting! He did really.’

definitions.definition: (UK) Being a graduate or alumnus of a school, especially a public school.
(heading) Of an earlier time.
Tiresome after prolonged repetition.

quote.text: Rik: But even great shtick can get old real fast: the dreaded Saturday Night Live syndrome.Jim: Randomness can help - many Living Books have characters that do different things each time you click on them.

quote.text: John and I built a small stone house on the head of “Bonetta” Canyon and had a hog killing time all by ourselves. Hunting was our delight at first, until it became old.

definitions.definition: Said of subdued colors, particularly reds, pinks and oranges, as if they had faded over time.
A grammatical intensifier, often used in describing something positive, and combined with another adjective.
(informal, of a person) Indicating affection and familiarity.

definitions.definition: Designed for a mature audience; unsuitable for children below a certain age.

definitions.definition: (with the, invariable plural only) People who are old; old beings; the older generation, taken as a group.
(slang) A person older than oneself, especially an adult in relation to a teenager.
(slang, most often plural) One's parents.
(Australia, uncountable) A typically dark-coloured lager brewed by the traditional top-fermentation method.
